unit: Unit 1: Historical Thinking, Geography, and Medieval Foundations
lesson: Lesson 2: Geography, Regions, and Historical Change
notes: All required passages, data, and schematic map descriptions are embedded. Correct answer positions vary and Moodle shuffles choices.

questions.name: F01 Physical geography
questions.prompt_html: Which example is part of physical geography?
choices: A mountain range
A national border
A spoken language
A trade agreement

questions.name: F02 Human geography
questions.prompt_html: Which example is part of human geography?
choices: Annual rainfall
A river valley
A network of market towns
A mountain pass

questions.name: F03 Region
questions.prompt_html: What is a region?
choices: Any place surrounded by water
An area grouped by shared characteristics
A location with no human activity
A border that never changes

questions.name: F04 Strategic location
questions.prompt_html: Which definition best matches strategic location?
choices: A place with identical physical features
A place far from all routes
A climate with steady rainfall
A place valuable for movement, defense, or trade

questions.name: F05 Cultural diffusion
questions.prompt_html: What is cultural diffusion?
choices: The spread of ideas, customs, technologies, or beliefs
The measurement of elevation
The isolation of every community
The legal creation of a border

questions.name: S01 River corridor map
questions.prompt_html:
Study the schematic map description.

A navigable river runs from inland farms to a coastal port. Three market towns stand along the river; steep mountains rise east and west of the valley.

Which map detail most directly explains why the market towns formed along the river?
choices: The mountains have steep slopes
The river connects inland farms to the port
The valley lies between two mountain ranges
The port is located at the coast

questions.name: S02 Mountain barrier
questions.prompt_html:
Study the travel table.

RouteDistanceTypical travel time
Across the mountain pass80 km5 days
Along the river valley120 km3 days

Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: Distance alone determines travel time
Mountains always prevent movement
Terrain and transportation routes can matter more than distance
River travel is impossible through valleys

questions.name: S03 Port trade data
questions.prompt_html:
Study the port records.

YearShips arrivingImported goods recorded
900183 types
950317 types
10004611 types

Which statement accurately interprets the evidence?
choices: The port's exchange network expanded over the period
The port stopped receiving ships
Imported goods became less varied
The table proves every resident became wealthy

questions.name: S04 Climate comparison
questions.prompt_html:
Study the climate data.

PlaceAnnual rainGrowing season
A750 mm210 days
B280 mm120 days

If all other conditions were similar, which inference is most reasonable?
choices: Place B must have a larger population
Place A likely offers stronger conditions for rain-fed farming
Place A cannot support trade
Place B has no possible human settlement

questions.name: S05 Settlement distribution
questions.prompt_html:
Read the map key and observations.

  • Large settlements: 6, all beside rivers or coasts
  • Small settlements: 14, including 5 in uplands
  • Major roads: connect the six large settlements

Which claim is best supported?
choices: Every upland was uninhabited
Roads caused all rivers to form
Access to water and transportation is associated with larger settlements
Coastal settlement was legally required

questions.name: S06 Strait map
questions.prompt_html:
Study the schematic.

Two large seas are connected by a narrow strait. City X stands beside the strait, and shipping routes from three regions pass it.

Why is City X strategically located?
choices: It can influence movement between the two seas
It is isolated from regional exchange
Its climate must be identical to every nearby place
The strait prevents all cultural diffusion

questions.name: S07 Migration evidence
questions.prompt_html:
Study the sequence.

Three years of drought → repeated harvest failures → food prices rise → families move toward a wetter river valley.

Which factor is the clearest geographic push factor?
choices: The wetter river valley
The movement of families
The rise of a new language
The drought and harvest failures

questions.name: S08 Trade network change
questions.prompt_html:
Compare the two network descriptions.

Map A, 900: Inland Town M connects to one nearby village.

Map B, 1050: A bridge and road connect Town M to a river port and four villages.

What changed?
choices: Town M became more isolated
Transportation improvements increased Town M's connections
The river disappeared
All trade shifted away from Town M

questions.name: S09 Opportunity and constraint
questions.prompt_html:
Read the geographic profile.

A community lies in a fertile valley protected by mountains. One narrow pass is closed by snow for part of each winter.

Which answer correctly identifies both an opportunity and a constraint?
choices: Opportunity: winter snow; constraint: fertile soil
Opportunity: no contact; constraint: protection
Opportunity: fertile farmland and defense; constraint: seasonal travel limits
Opportunity: mountain height; constraint: the existence of a valley

questions.name: S10 Source limitation
questions.prompt_html:
Read the source note.

A merchant's letter praises a port as “the finest market in the world.” The merchant hoped to persuade partners to invest there.

What limitation should a historian consider?
choices: The investment purpose may encourage exaggeration
The letter cannot reveal anything about trade
All merchants lived in the same region
The quotation proves the port was the world's largest

questions.name: A01 Geography and choice
questions.prompt_html: Which statement avoids geographic determinism?
choices: Mountains force every society to remain isolated
Climate alone explains every political change
Geography creates opportunities and constraints, but people make choices within them
River valleys always produce identical societies

questions.name: A02 Best evidence
questions.prompt_html: A student claims that a river helped a medieval town grow. Which evidence would best support the claim?
choices: Records showing rising river trade and population over the same period
A modern opinion that rivers are attractive
A map with no date or labels
A list of rulers unrelated to the town

questions.name: A03 Causal reasoning
questions.prompt_html: A new bridge was built, and trade later increased. What additional evidence would most strengthen the claim that the bridge contributed to the increase?
choices: A description of mountain colors
Records showing merchants began using the bridge to reach new markets
Proof that trade existed centuries earlier
A statement that every bridge increases trade

questions.name: A04 Compare regions
questions.prompt_html: Region A has navigable rivers and open plains. Region B has steep mountains and few passes. Which comparison is most defensible?
choices: Region B cannot have any culture
Region A must defeat Region B in war
Both regions will develop identically
Movement may be easier in Region A, while passes may concentrate travel in Region B

questions.name: A05 Human response
questions.prompt_html: Farmers in a dry region construct irrigation canals. Which explanation best shows interaction between physical and human geography?
choices: People changed how water was distributed in response to limited rainfall
Rainfall became a political border
The canals prove climate no longer matters
Physical geography prevented every human decision

questions.name: A06 CER reasoning
questions.prompt_html:
Claim: A coastal city's location encouraged cultural diffusion.

Evidence: Port records list merchants and goods from four regions.

Which sentence is the strongest reasoning?
choices: The city had buildings near the water
Regular contact among merchants created opportunities for ideas and customs to spread
Four is larger than three
All coastal cities develop the same culture

questions.name: A07 Changing regions
questions.prompt_html: Why might historians define the same place as part of different regions?
choices: Regions are always errors
Physical features change every day
Regional boundaries depend on the question and shared characteristics being studied
A place can have only one characteristic

questions.name: A08 Settlement choice
questions.prompt_html: A ruler must choose between Site A beside a navigable river but exposed to flooding and Site B on a high plateau with little water. What is the best analysis?
choices: Site A offers transport and water but needs flood management; Site B offers elevation but faces water limits
Site A has no constraint
Site B has no opportunity
Geography makes the choice automatic

questions.name: A09 Network consequence
questions.prompt_html: A previously isolated valley gains an all-season road to a port. Which is the most plausible historical consequence?
choices: All local traditions immediately disappear
The valley's climate changes
Every resident becomes a merchant
Exchange of goods and ideas is likely to increase

questions.name: A10 Defensible conclusion
questions.prompt_html: Maps show towns clustered beside rivers, but tax records are incomplete. Which conclusion is most defensible?
choices: Rivers were the only cause of every town
The maps suggest river access influenced settlement, but more evidence is needed about other causes
The missing records prove maps are false
No conclusion can be formed from geographic evidence
